sources.name: ITF Rules of Tennis 2026
claims: Rule 5 (Score in a Game): Standard game scoring, server score called first.
Rule 17 (The Server & Receiver): Receiver readiness and service boundary rules.
Rule 24 (Player Loses Point): Ball touching player, double bounce, net touch constitute immediate loss of point.
Rule 29 (Continuous play & rest): 25 seconds between points, prompt match continuation.
sources.limitations: Covers official competitive tennis rules. Club-level friendly matches may operate with local modifications.

sources.name: USTA FAC The Code - The Players' Guide to Fair Play
claims: Section 1-5: A player calls all shots on their own side of the net promptly and clearly.
Section 6-10: Any ball that cannot be called out with 100% certainty must be treated as in (benefit of the doubt to opponent).
Section 11-15: Score disputes must revert to the last agreed-upon score; let calls cannot be made on clear out balls.
sources.limitations: Self-officiating code for unofficiated matches; distinct from chair-umpired tournaments.

sources.name: ITF Tennis Technical & Equipment Guidelines: Overgrips & Racket Mechanics
claims: Overgrips add 0.5mm to 0.75mm to handle circumference, affecting torsional stability on off-center impacts.
Dry-type polyurethane overgrips excel at sweat absorption without losing traction, whereas tacky grips provide adhesion in low-humidity conditions.
sources.limitations: Grip preference varies with player hand size, climate, and sweat gland physiology.

sources.name: USTA Equipment Care: Overgrips, Grip Sizes & Moisture Management
claims: Wristbands block sweat descending from forearm to palm, reducing hand slipping by up to 60%.
A 3-step change protocol ensures even tension without overlapping ridges that cause blisters.
sources.limitations: Equipment maintenance guideline, not a guarantee against all mishits.

sources.name: ITF Biomechanics of the Tennis Serve: Toss Placement & Release Consistency
claims: The optimal toss apex is roughly 15 to 30 cm above maximum racquet reach, giving a predictable falling velocity.
Fingertip release without wrist flexion prevents unintended rotational spin on the tossed ball.
sources.limitations: Individual height, wind conditions, and stance (platform vs pinpoint) modify optimal toss parameters.

sources.name: USTA Player Development: Toss Consistency, Height, and Placement Standards
claims: Flat serves require toss at 12:30 to 1:00 clock position in front of baseline; kick serves require toss at 11:30 to 12:00 over head.
Synchronizing toss release with knee bend initiation stabilizes trunk posture and trophy position.
sources.limitations: Self-training drills; high wind necessitates lower toss height adjustment.

sources.name: USTA Warrior Doubles Strategy: Defending & Attacking the Middle Ball
claims: Forehand in the middle takes priority when both players are parallel at the baseline or net.
When crosscourt diagonal player has better approach angle, clear single-syllable voice call ('Mine/Me') overrides default position.
sources.limitations: Applies to standard doubles formations; Australian or I-formation requires pre-point hand signal agreement.

sources.name: ITF Doubles Tactics & Communication Protocols
claims: Indecision on center balls accounts for over 28% of unforced errors in amateur doubles rallies.
Early non-verbal cues and committed loud calls eliminate racket clashes and hesitation.
sources.limitations: Partner chemistry and shared understanding required; adapt when playing with unfamiliar guest partners.

sources.name: ITF Sport Science & Medicine: Lower Limb Loading and Split-Step Mechanics
claims: Landing on the forefoot (balls of the feet) with knee and hip flexion reduces peak ground reaction impact transmitted to patellar tendon by up to 45% compared to heel-first landing.
Stiff-legged landing creates excessive shear forces across the anterior cruciate ligament and meniscus.
sources.limitations: Biomechanical principles; not an individualized medical treatment or guarantee against sports injuries.

sources.name: NHS / Newcastle Hospitals Guidance: Knee Joint Protection and Deceleration in Racquet Sports
claims: Gradual deceleration and proper footwear with adequate cushioning protect knee cartilage from repetitive concussive trauma.
Persistent swelling, locking, giving way, or acute pain during weight-bearing warrants immediate rest and medical evaluation.
sources.limitations: General clinical guidance. Discontinue play immediately upon acute joint pain or instability.
